scenario.name: Microsoft & CISA DFIR — SMB ADMIN$ Share, PSEXESVC Named Pipe & Service Install Forensics (EID 5145 / 7045)
scenario.overview: Imagine an intruder standing in a corridor who drops a remote worker kit onto a neighbor administrative loading dock, phones the shift foreman to register that kit as a brand-new building service, and hooks up a control tube plus three pneumatic speaking tubes (one to send typed orders, one to hear normal replies, and one to hear error shouts) straight back to their own desk, leaving a crisp four-step trail even if they repaint the kit name. In this scenario (T1021.002, Microsoft & CISA DFIR, SMB ADMIN$ Share, PSEXESVC Named Pipe & Service Install Forensics , EID 5145 / 7045), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: sMB ADMIN$ Share Write, then remote Service Installation via SCM, then named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering SMB ADMIN$ Share Write, then Remote Service Installation via SCM, then Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 17 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: SMB ADMIN$ Share Write & IPC$ svcctl RPC Bind (Security EventID 5140 & 5145)
stages.subtitle: Lateral Movement (T1021.002 - Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares)
stages.description: From a neighboring workstation, the intruder unlocks the target administrative loading bay, drops a packaged service helper onto the dock, and opens the shift-foreman intercom channel to prepare an installation order. The attacker executes PsExec.exe \\10.10.20.15 -s cmd.exe. The target host logs Security EventID 5140 (Network share object accessed) and EventID 5145 (Detailed File Share Access) showing WriteData (AccessMask 0x2) of PSEXESVC.exe into the \\*\ADMIN$ share (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe), followed by an IPC$ access to the svcctl named pipe (logged in WinEvent Event 5145 with EventID=5145 , Detailed File Share Audit, ShareName=\\*\ADMIN$ , C:\Windows, RelativeTargetName=PSEXESVC.exe, AccessMask=0x2 , WriteData so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes PsExec.exe -accepteula \\10.10.20.15 -s cmd.exe (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1021.002 during "SMB ADMIN$ Share Write & IPC$ svcctl RPC Bind , Security EventID 5140 & 5145", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). Next, the follow-up artifact Security EventID 5145: ShareName=\\*\ADMIN$ RelativeTargetName=PSEXESVC.exe AccessMask=0x2 (WriteData) runs (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1021.002 during "SMB ADMIN$ Share Write & IPC$ svcctl RPC Bind , Security EventID 5140 & 5145", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SMB2 Write \\*\ADMIN$\PSEXESVC.exe & IPC$\svcctl bind / ⇠#1 ACK 5145) from Node ① (#1 Operator Host (PsExec.exe)) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PSEXESVC.exe & Named Pipes).

stages.title: Stage 2: Remote Service Installation via SCM CreateServiceW (System EventID 7045 & Security EventID 4697)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1569.002 - System Services: Service Execution)
stages.description: Receiving the installation order over the foreman intercom, the building shift supervisor writes a brand-new service entry onto the master roster and starts the uploaded helper with full building-wide master keys. Over the \pipe\svcctl RPC interface, the Service Control Manager (services.exe) invokes CreateServiceW and logs System EventID 7045 (A service was installed in the system) and Security EventID 4697 with ServiceName="PSEXESVC", ImagePath="%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe", ServiceType="user mode service" (0x10), and StartType="demand start" (0x3) (logged in WinEvent Event 7045 with EventID=7045 , System SCM / 4697 , Security, ServiceName=PSEXESVC, ServiceFileName=%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, ServiceAccount=LocalSystem so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes RPC svcctl: RCreateServiceW(lpServiceName="PSEXESVC", lpBinaryPathName="%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe") (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1569.002 during "Remote Service Installation via SCM CreateServiceW , System EventID 7045 & Security EventID 4697", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). Next, the follow-up artifact System EventID 7045: Service Name=PSEXESVC, Service File Name=%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, Account Name=LocalSystem runs (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1569.002 during "Remote Service Installation via SCM CreateServiceW , System EventID 7045 & Security EventID 4697", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 7045) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 SMB :445 ADMIN$ & IPC$ Share), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PSEXESVC.exe & Named Pipes).

keySpecs.value: System EventID 7045: Service Name=PSEXESVC, Service File Name=%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, Account Name=LocalSystem

Alert on System EventID 7045 and Security EventID 4697 where ServiceFileName references %SystemRoot%, ADMIN$, cmd.exe /c, powershell.exe, or random 8-character service names (Impacket smbexec/psexec).

stages.title: Stage 3: Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection (Sysmon EventID 17 & 18)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1569.002 - Sysmon EventID 17/18 Named Pipe Forensics)
stages.description: Even if the intruder paints a brand-new cover name over the worker kit to dodge simple name filters, the live helper still opens one master control pipe and three matching pneumatic speaking tubes (one for incoming commands, one for normal output, and one for error messages), creating a dead-giveaway architectural fingerprint. Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC.exe creates a control pipe and three I/O redirection named pipes matching \PSEXESVC-<Host>-<PID>-stdin, -stdout, and -stderr. Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated) and EventID 18 (PipeConnected) capture the exact PipeName and Image regardless of service renaming (logged in Sysmon Event 17 with EventID=17 , PipeCreated / 18 , PipeConnected, Image=C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, PipeNamePattern=\PSEXESVC-<HOST>-<PID>-{stdin,stdout,stderr}, SpawnedChildProcess=C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe , NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated): PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Sysmon EventID 17 , PipeCreated: PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin via System / Runtime Ex so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1569.002 during "Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection , Sysmon EventID 17 & 18" , Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated): PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdout runs (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Sysmon EventID 17 , PipeCreated: PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdout via System / Runtime E so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1569.002 during "Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection , Sysmon EventID 17 & 18" , Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe creating \PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin / ⇠#3 ACK 17) from Node ③ (#3 SMB :445 ADMIN$ & IPC$ Share) to Node ④ (#4 services.exe (SCM PID 612)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PSEXESVC.exe & Named Pipes).

steps.storyAnalogy: Even if the intruder paints a brand-new cover name over the worker kit to dodge simple name filters, the live helper still opens one master control pipe and three matching pneumatic speaking tubes (one for incoming commands, one for normal output, and one for error messages), creating a dead-giveaway architectural fingerprint.
steps.simpleExplanation: Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC.exe creates a control pipe and three I/O redirection named pipes matching \PSEXESVC-<Host>-<PID>-stdin, -stdout, and -stderr. Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated) and EventID 18 (PipeConnected) capture the exact PipeName and Image regardless of service renaming (logged in Sysmon Event 17 with EventID=17 , PipeCreated / 18 , PipeConnected, Image=C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, PipeNamePattern=\PSEXESVC-<HOST>-<PID>-{stdin,stdout,stderr}, SpawnedChildProcess=C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe , NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Under the hood, the observed step executes Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated): PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Sysmon EventID 17 , PipeCreated: PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin via System / Runtime Ex so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1569.002 during "Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection , Sysmon EventID 17 & 18" , Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated): PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdout runs (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Sysmon EventID 17 , PipeCreated: PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdout via System / Runtime E so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1569.002 during "Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection , Sysmon EventID 17 & 18" , Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution).
steps.diagramAlignment: On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 across the topology from Operator Host , PsExec.exe and SMB :445 ADMIN$ & IPC$ Share toward services.exe , SCM PID 612 and EID 5145, 7045 & Sysmon EID 17/18.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Documented in Sysmon Event 17 (recording EventID=17 , PipeCreated / 18 , PipeConnected, Image=C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, PipeNamePattern=\PSEXESVC-<HOST>-<PID>-{stdin,stdout,stderr}, SpawnedChildProcess=C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe , NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM under T1569.002): Monitor Sysmon EventID 17 and EventID 18 for named pipes ending in -stdin, -stdout, -stderr, or matching \RemCom_communicaton, \csexec, and \paexec.
